turns.doctor_question: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. Thank you for coming in today. What brings you to see me?
turns.patient_response: Hi. Well, I'm here because I've been having this issue with elevators. I mean, I know they aren't really dangerous, but... whenever I have to get in one, I just get really scared, like I'm going to be trapped in there. I just can't make myself feel normal about it.

symptom_reasoning.S062: The patient describes intense, disproportionate fear of being trapped in elevators despite knowing they are not truly dangerous, consistent with situational specific phobic fear.

turns.doctor_question: Besides elevators, are there other situations or places that make you feel similarly anxious or scared?
turns.patient_response: No, not really. It's pretty much just elevators. I mean, I work in construction, so I'm in and out of all kinds of tight spaces or high up on sites all the time, and none of that bothers me. It's really just... yeah, just elevators that make me feel that way.

symptom_reasoning.S062: The patient confirms that elevators specifically provoke fear and anxiety, while other situations like tight spaces or heights do not bother them.

turns.doctor_question: How long have you been experiencing this fear of elevators?
turns.patient_response: I'd say it's been going on for about 11 months now. It started right after we lost our house and had to move into this upper-floor apartment.

symptom_reasoning.S062: The patient confirms experiencing a fear of elevators (Situational Type specific phobia) that has been ongoing for approximately 11 months.

turns.doctor_question: You mentioned you work in tight spaces without anxiety. Can you tell me more about what specifically frightens you in elevators? Is it the enclosed space itself, or is it something else about elevators?
turns.patient_response: I don't think it's just the space itself, since I do fine at work. It's more... well, it happens right away. As soon as those doors start sliding shut, my chest gets tight and my hands start sweating. All I can think is, 'I need out.' And that happens even if it's only going up a few floors. It just hits me instantly.

symptom_reasoning.S063: The patient describes an immediate physiological fear and panic response (tight chest, sweating hands, urge to escape) triggered instantly when elevator doors begin to shut.

turns.doctor_question: When you need to go to your apartment or other places that require using an elevator, what do you typically do?
turns.patient_response: Most days I just take the stairs. I do it at our apartment building, and I do it on job sites whenever I can. If an elevator or some kind of lift is literally the only way up... well, I either ask my boss to put me on a different task, or I'll only ride it if someone I really trust is standing right there in the car with me.

symptom_reasoning.S064: The patient actively avoids elevators by taking the stairs or requesting different tasks, and relies on a trusted companion as a safety signal when forced to ride one.

turns.doctor_question: When you're in that elevator and your chest gets tight and your hands sweat, do you ever experience other physical symptoms like your heart racing, difficulty breathing, dizziness, or a feeling that something terrible might happen to you?
turns.patient_response: No, I wouldn't say all that. I mean, my heart doesn't really race or anything, and I don't get dizzy or feel like I can't breathe. It's pretty much just the sweating and that tight feeling in my chest. I don't really think something terrible is going to happen to me... I just really, really want to get out of there.

turns.doctor_question: You mentioned your chest gets tight and your hands sweat in elevators. When this happens, does your heart rate feel noticeably faster than normal, or do you feel like you can't catch your breath?
turns.patient_response: No, like I said before, my heart rate doesn't really speed up, and I don't have any trouble breathing. It's just the tight chest and the sweaty hands. I don't feel like I can't catch my breath or anything like that.

turns.doctor_question: Before you even get into an elevator—like when you know you're about to have to use one—do you start feeling anxious or scared ahead of time, or does the fear only kick in once you're actually inside and the doors are closing?
turns.patient_response: I don't really get worked up beforehand, no. I mean, if I know I have to take one, I don't sit around worrying about it or anything. It's really just... when I actually step inside and those doors shut, that's when the tight chest and the sweating starts. But before that? Walking up to it or just knowing I have to use it? No, I'm fine then.

symptom_reasoning.S063: The patient confirms that stepping inside the elevator and having the doors shut immediately triggers physiological panic symptoms including a tight chest and sweating.

turns.doctor_question: When you're in the elevator and feel that tight chest and sweating, does the fear or discomfort build up gradually over a few minutes, or does it come on very suddenly and intensely right away?
turns.patient_response: I wouldn't really say it's sudden and intense, no. It's just... once the doors shut, I notice my chest feels tight and my hands are sweating. It doesn't really build up over a few minutes either—mostly because elevator rides aren't usually that long anyway. It just kind of starts when I'm stuck in there and stays about the same until I can walk out.

symptom_reasoning.S063: The patient confirms experiencing an immediate anxiety response (chest tightness and sweating) as soon as the elevator doors shut.
